Achievement Indicators:
Situational: Understand the impact of context on communication, including formal and informal contexts.
Engagement: Show sensitivity to the needs of the listener by addressing different audiences respectfully.
Year-End: The student understands how context, including formal and informal settings, affects communication, and shows sensitivity to listeners’ needs by addressing different audiences respectfully.
Student Statement: I can tell what a situation needs.
Conditions: Role-plays with clear contrasts; teacher-provided examples.
Look Fors:
## Situational
- Recognizes that different situations call for different tones.
- Sorts examples into formal and informal, with reasons.
## Engagement
- Identifies different audiences and suitable language for each.
Awareness - Description: Names a convention for a context.
Awareness - Student Quote: A presentation is formal, so no slang.
Evidence Opportunities: A formal/informal sort of example messages, with a reason for each.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust interactions to reflect the situation, audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Situational: Understand the impact of context on communication, including formal and informal contexts.
Engagement: Show sensitivity to the needs of the listener by addressing different audiences respectfully.
Year-End: The student understands how context, including formal and informal settings, affects communication, and shows sensitivity to listeners’ needs by addressing different audiences respectfully.
Student Statement: I can explain how the setting changes how I communicate.
Conditions: Less obvious contexts (a group chat, a class discussion, an email to a teacher, an interview).
Look Fors:
## Situational
- Explains how setting, relationship, and purpose change communication.
- Identifies when a mismatch would cause a problem.
## Engagement
- Adjusts language for a listener’s needs (age, background knowledge) when planning.
Awareness - Student Quote: In an email to a teacher, you need a greeting and full sentences, or it seems rude.
Evidence Opportunities: Rewrite one message for three contexts and explain each change.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust interactions to reflect the situation, audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Situational: Understand the impact of context on communication, including formal and informal contexts.
Engagement: Show sensitivity to the needs of the listener by addressing different audiences respectfully.
Year-End: The student understands how context, including formal and informal settings, affects communication, and shows sensitivity to listeners’ needs by addressing different audiences respectfully.
Student Statement: I can adjust what I say for my listener.
Conditions: Real audiences and situations (a guest speaker, younger students, community members); mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Situational
- Adjusts formality for the context in planned interactions.
- Recognizes afterward when their communication didn’t fit.
## Engagement
- Shows sensitivity to listeners’ needs (checks understanding, rephrases, avoids jargon) in most planned interactions.
Awareness - Description: Explains an adjustment for a listener.
Awareness - Student Quote: Our guest didn’t know much about gaming, so I explained the terms first.
Evidence Opportunities: A real-audience task (an invitation, a thank-you, a talk to another class), then a reflection on choices made.
Left for June: Adjusting in unplanned situations and with unfamiliar audiences.

Skill Descriptor: Critically reflect on the contributions of others.
Achievement Indicators:
Message: Determine what information is important, relevant, and worthy of further consideration.
Impact: Identify and respond to the perspective and worldview presented within a speaker’s contribution.
Year-End: The student determines which information in others’ contributions is important, relevant, and worth further thought, and identifies and responds to the perspective and worldview behind a speaker’s contribution.
Student Statement: I can connect what others say to my own thinking.
Conditions: Structured discussions; response stems.
Look Fors:
## Message
- Notes key points from a speaker.
- Connects others’ ideas to their own thinking.
## Impact
- Explains how a peer’s idea changed or confirmed their understanding after the discussion.
Awareness - Student Quote: Jai’s point made me rethink my answer.
Evidence Opportunities: A before-and-after thinking chart around a discussion.

Skill Descriptor: Critically reflect on the contributions of others.
Achievement Indicators:
Message: Determine what information is important, relevant, and worthy of further consideration.
Impact: Identify and respond to the perspective and worldview presented within a speaker’s contribution.
Year-End: The student determines which information in others’ contributions is important, relevant, and worth further thought, and identifies and responds to the perspective and worldview behind a speaker’s contribution.
Student Statement: I can pick out what’s worth thinking more about.
Conditions: Discussions, guest speakers, and recorded talks; note-taking routines.
Look Fors:
## Message
- Sorts information as important, relevant, or not.
- Identifies one idea worth exploring further and says why.
## Impact
- Identifies the perspective a speaker is coming from (“She’s speaking as a farmer”).
Awareness - Student Quote: The part about water use is worth looking into because it affects everyone here.
Evidence Opportunities: A listening log: key points, one idea worth further thought, the speaker’s perspective.

Skill Descriptor: Critically reflect on the contributions of others.
Achievement Indicators:
Message: Determine what information is important, relevant, and worthy of further consideration.
Impact: Identify and respond to the perspective and worldview presented within a speaker’s contribution.
Year-End: The student determines which information in others’ contributions is important, relevant, and worth further thought, and identifies and responds to the perspective and worldview behind a speaker’s contribution.
Student Statement: I can respond to the worldview behind what someone says.
Conditions: Varied speakers, including some with views different from students’; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Message
- Judges importance and relevance consistently with familiar topics, and explains why something deserves more thought.
## Impact
- Identifies the worldview behind a contribution and responds respectfully by agreeing, questioning, or extending.
Awareness - Student Quote: He sees the forest as jobs, and I see it as a place to hike, so we’re not arguing about the same thing.
Evidence Opportunities: A response to a guest speaker or podcast: key ideas, the speaker’s worldview, and my response.
Left for June: Identifying worldviews that are implied rather than stated, and responding during the discussion rather than afterward.

Skill Descriptor: Apply knowledge of advanced word structures as a word-solving strategy.
Achievement Indicators:
Word Solving/ Knowledge: Apply knowledge of syllable patterns to decode complex multi-syllabic words.
Morphology & Etymology: Continue to use Anglo-Saxon and Latin morpheme knowledge to solve words.
Year-End: The student applies syllable patterns to decode complex multisyllabic words and uses Anglo-Saxon and Latin morphemes to solve words, explaining how word structure helped.
Student Statement: I can break longer words into parts I know.
Conditions: Three- and four-syllable words; affix charts available.
Look Fors:
## Word Solving/ Knowledge
- Decodes multisyllabic words using the six syllable types and common division patterns.
## Morphology & Etymology
- Uses Anglo-Saxon prefixes and suffixes to decode words and get at their meaning.
- Recognizes a few common Latin roots (port, rupt, struct) once taught.
Awareness - Student Quote: I took off ‘un-’ and ‘-able’ and read the middle first.
Evidence Opportunities: A word sort and read-aloud of 15 to 20 words, with a think-aloud on three.

Skill Descriptor: Apply knowledge of advanced word structures as a word-solving strategy.
Achievement Indicators:
Word Solving/ Knowledge: Apply knowledge of syllable patterns to decode complex multi-syllabic words.
Morphology & Etymology: Continue to use Anglo-Saxon and Latin morpheme knowledge to solve words.
Year-End: The student applies syllable patterns to decode complex multisyllabic words and uses Anglo-Saxon and Latin morphemes to solve words, explaining how word structure helped.
Student Statement: I can use Latin roots to help solve words.
Conditions: Vocabulary from shared class texts and other subjects; root charts available.
Look Fors:
## Word Solving/ Knowledge
- Decodes four- and five-syllable words, including unstressed (schwa) syllables, trying another split when needed.
## Morphology & Etymology
- Uses common Latin roots and prefixes (inter-, trans-, sub-, pre-) to decode and infer meaning.
- Notices words that share a root (transport, portable, import).
Awareness - Student Quote: ‘Rupt’ means break, so ‘erupt’ is when something breaks out.
Evidence Opportunities: A root-family word web plus a decoding task using words from other subjects.

Skill Descriptor: Apply knowledge of advanced word structures as a word-solving strategy.
Achievement Indicators:
Word Solving/ Knowledge: Apply knowledge of syllable patterns to decode complex multi-syllabic words.
Morphology & Etymology: Continue to use Anglo-Saxon and Latin morpheme knowledge to solve words.
Year-End: The student applies syllable patterns to decode complex multisyllabic words and uses Anglo-Saxon and Latin morphemes to solve words, explaining how word structure helped.
Student Statement: I can solve complex words when I read and explain how.
Conditions: Complex words met in shared class texts across subjects; occasional prompts.
Look Fors:
## Word Solving/ Knowledge
- Decodes complex multisyllabic words in connected text, independently most of the time.
## Morphology & Etymology
- Combines Anglo-Saxon and Latin morpheme knowledge to solve unfamiliar words.
- May misapply a root that only looks similar.
Awareness - Student Quote: ‘Inter’ means between and ‘rupt’ means break, so ‘interrupt’ is breaking in between someone.
Evidence Opportunities: A conference during independent reading on two words the student solved.
Left for June: Applying word structure flexibly across varied texts and explaining it consistently, including noticing when a “root” is misleading.

Skill Descriptor: Read an increasing variety of text with accuracy and expression, both silently and aloud.
Achievement Indicators:
Expression: Read a variety of familiar and less familiar texts with changes in intonation, tone, and volume.
Rhythm & Phrasing: Read internal and end punctuation of familiar texts with confidence.
Smoothness: Read most texts with minimal hesitation and self-correct with minimal prompting.
Automaticity: Read a variety of texts accurately and effortlessly.
Year-End: The student reads familiar and less familiar texts accurately, effortlessly, and with expression, reads punctuation confidently, and self-corrects with minimal prompting.
Student Statement: I can read familiar texts with expression.
Conditions: Rehearsed, familiar texts, with some first reads.
Look Fors:
## Expression
- Changes tone and volume to match meaning in familiar texts.
## Rhythm & Phrasing
- Reads commas and end punctuation; hesitates at dashes, semicolons, and ellipses.
## Smoothness
- Self-corrects when prompted.
## Automaticity
- Reads common multisyllabic words at a steady pace in familiar texts.
Awareness - Student Quote: I slowed down at the dash because it’s like a pause.
Evidence Opportunities: A one-minute oral reading with a fluency rubric (expression, phrasing, smoothness, pace).

Skill Descriptor: Read an increasing variety of text with accuracy and expression, both silently and aloud.
Achievement Indicators:
Expression: Read a variety of familiar and less familiar texts with changes in intonation, tone, and volume.
Rhythm & Phrasing: Read internal and end punctuation of familiar texts with confidence.
Smoothness: Read most texts with minimal hesitation and self-correct with minimal prompting.
Automaticity: Read a variety of texts accurately and effortlessly.
Year-End: The student reads familiar and less familiar texts accurately, effortlessly, and with expression, reads punctuation confidently, and self-corrects with minimal prompting.
Student Statement: I can read less familiar texts with expression.
Conditions: First reads of shared class texts in several genres.
Look Fors:
## Expression
- Brings expression to a less familiar text after one read-through.
## Rhythm & Phrasing
- Reads internal punctuation with growing confidence.
## Smoothness
- Hesitations are brief; self-corrects with a light prompt such as a pause or look.
## Automaticity
- Reads accurately, slowing occasionally on unfamiliar words.
Awareness - Student Quote: I read it quietly first, so I’d know where the sad part was.
Evidence Opportunities: Readers’ theatre or a poetry reading of a text new to the student.

Skill Descriptor: Read an increasing variety of text with accuracy and expression, both silently and aloud.
Achievement Indicators:
Expression: Read a variety of familiar and less familiar texts with changes in intonation, tone, and volume.
Rhythm & Phrasing: Read internal and end punctuation of familiar texts with confidence.
Smoothness: Read most texts with minimal hesitation and self-correct with minimal prompting.
Automaticity: Read a variety of texts accurately and effortlessly.
Year-End: The student reads familiar and less familiar texts accurately, effortlessly, and with expression, reads punctuation confidently, and self-corrects with minimal prompting.
Student Statement: I can read most texts smoothly without much help.
Conditions: Varied texts, including first reads and texts from other subjects; silent and oral.
Look Fors:
## Expression
- Reads less familiar texts with expression most of the time.
## Rhythm & Phrasing
- Reads internal and end punctuation in familiar texts with confidence.
## Smoothness
- Minimal hesitation; self-corrects mostly without prompting.
## Automaticity
- Accurate and effortless in most texts; dense subject-area texts may slow the pace.
Awareness - Student Quote: That sentence didn’t make sense, so I went back and reread it.
Evidence Opportunities: A recorded reading compared with November’s, plus a self-assessment.
Left for June: Effortless, expressive reading across a wider variety of texts, including dense subject-area texts.

Skill Descriptor: Recognize how different strategies are used to determine the meaning of words.
Achievement Indicators:
Strategy Flexibility: Begin using multiple strategies, with guidance, to determine new vocabulary.
Semantic Knowledge: Use sentence and text features, in addition to context and morphology, to find the meaning of unknown words.
Figurative Language: Use knowledge of common figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, idiom, imagery) to contribute to understanding of a text.
Year-End: The student uses multiple strategies with guidance, draws on sentence and text features along with context and morphology to find the meaning of unknown words, and uses common figurative language to deepen understanding of a text.
Student Statement: I can try more than one strategy.
Conditions: Shared class texts; strategy anchor chart available.
Look Fors:
## Strategy Flexibility
- Uses one strategy, then tries a second when prompted.
## Semantic Knowledge
- Uses context clues and word parts to understand new words.
## Figurative Language
- Identifies similes, metaphors, and idioms, and tells literal from figurative meaning.
Awareness - Student Quote: Context didn’t help, so I looked at the word parts.
Evidence Opportunities: A word-detective log: word, my guess, clue I used, check.

Skill Descriptor: Recognize how different strategies are used to determine the meaning of words.
Achievement Indicators:
Strategy Flexibility: Begin using multiple strategies, with guidance, to determine new vocabulary.
Semantic Knowledge: Use sentence and text features, in addition to context and morphology, to find the meaning of unknown words.
Figurative Language: Use knowledge of common figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, idiom, imagery) to contribute to understanding of a text.
Year-End: The student uses multiple strategies with guidance, draws on sentence and text features along with context and morphology to find the meaning of unknown words, and uses common figurative language to deepen understanding of a text.
Student Statement: I can use sentence and text features too.
Conditions: Literary and informational texts; guided practice.
Look Fors:
## Strategy Flexibility
- Combines two strategies with guidance.
## Semantic Knowledge
- Uses sentence features (commas, dashes, or parentheses that signal a definition) and text features (glossaries, captions, sidebars, diagrams).
## Figurative Language
- Adds personification, hyperbole, and imagery, and explains what one example adds.
Awareness - Student Quote: The commas after ‘larvae’ explain it: baby insects.
Evidence Opportunities: An annotated passage marking which clue unlocked each word.

Skill Descriptor: Recognize how different strategies are used to determine the meaning of words.
Achievement Indicators:
Strategy Flexibility: Begin using multiple strategies, with guidance, to determine new vocabulary.
Semantic Knowledge: Use sentence and text features, in addition to context and morphology, to find the meaning of unknown words.
Figurative Language: Use knowledge of common figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, idiom, imagery) to contribute to understanding of a text.
Year-End: The student uses multiple strategies with guidance, draws on sentence and text features along with context and morphology to find the meaning of unknown words, and uses common figurative language to deepen understanding of a text.
Student Statement: I can combine strategies and use figurative language to understand more.
Conditions: More complex texts; less guidance.
Look Fors:
## Strategy Flexibility
- Chooses and combines strategies, still benefiting from guidance with difficult words.
## Semantic Knowledge
- Uses sentence and text features along with context and morphology to arrive at a meaning.
## Figurative Language
- Explains how figurative language adds to the meaning, mood, or theme of a text.
Awareness - Student Quote: The hyperbole about walking a million miles shows how tired he is, and that’s why he gives up.
Evidence Opportunities: A conference: one word the student figured out and one figurative phrase they explain.
Left for June: Choosing strategies with less guidance on difficult words, and using figurative language to support understanding across genres.

Skill Descriptor: Construct meaning from a variety of text considering the source, intended audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Literal Understanding: Summarize text and respond to literal questions using relevant examples from the text for support.
Inferential Understanding: Infer relationships among ideas to draw conclusions and make comparisons.
Text Intention: Compare stated or implied purposes of different writers writing on the same topic.
Year-End: The student summarizes and answers literal questions with relevant examples from the text, infers relationships among ideas to draw conclusions and make comparisons, and compares the stated or implied purposes of different writers on the same topic.
Student Statement: I can summarize and back it up.
Conditions: Single shared class texts; guided questions.
Look Fors:
## Literal Understanding
- Summarizes accurately.
- Begins to support literal answers with an example from the text.
## Inferential Understanding
- Draws conclusions from text clues and prior knowledge.
## Text Intention
- Determines one writer’s purpose and audience.
Awareness - Student Quote: It says on page 4 that the river flooded every spring.
Evidence Opportunities: A summary plus literal questions that require an example from the text.

Skill Descriptor: Construct meaning from a variety of text considering the source, intended audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Literal Understanding: Summarize text and respond to literal questions using relevant examples from the text for support.
Inferential Understanding: Infer relationships among ideas to draw conclusions and make comparisons.
Text Intention: Compare stated or implied purposes of different writers writing on the same topic.
Year-End: The student summarizes and answers literal questions with relevant examples from the text, infers relationships among ideas to draw conclusions and make comparisons, and compares the stated or implied purposes of different writers on the same topic.
Student Statement: I can see how ideas connect.
Conditions: Longer texts and paired texts on one topic; small-group and independent work.
Look Fors:
## Literal Understanding
- Supports literal answers with relevant examples consistently.
## Inferential Understanding
- Infers relationships among ideas (cause and effect, contrast, problem and solution).
## Text Intention
- Identifies each writer’s purpose in a pair of texts on the same topic.
Awareness - Student Quote: The drought caused the crops to fail, and that’s why the family moved.
Evidence Opportunities: Paired texts with an organizer for how ideas relate.

Skill Descriptor: Construct meaning from a variety of text considering the source, intended audience, and purpose.
Achievement Indicators:
Literal Understanding: Summarize text and respond to literal questions using relevant examples from the text for support.
Inferential Understanding: Infer relationships among ideas to draw conclusions and make comparisons.
Text Intention: Compare stated or implied purposes of different writers writing on the same topic.
Year-End: The student summarizes and answers literal questions with relevant examples from the text, infers relationships among ideas to draw conclusions and make comparisons, and compares the stated or implied purposes of different writers on the same topic.
Student Statement: I can compare what different writers are trying to do.
Conditions: Two or more texts on one topic from varied sources; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Literal Understanding
- Summarizes and supports answers with relevant examples across text types.
## Inferential Understanding
- Draws conclusions and makes comparisons across texts.
## Text Intention
- Compares writers’ stated purposes; comparing implied purposes may need a prompt.
Awareness - Student Quote: Both are about the new rink. The town’s page wants you to come; the news article wants you to know what it cost.
Evidence Opportunities: A comparison of two texts on one topic: summary of each, purpose of each, and how they differ.
Left for June: Comparing implied purposes independently and drawing comparisons across less familiar sources.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust and use a wide variety of strategies to make meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Attention Strategies: Use relevant questioning during reading to clarify understanding of the main ideas and supporting details.
Knowledge Strategies: Skim texts to locate textual evidence for predictions and inferences.
Monitoring Strategies: Apply self-correction strategies with prompting when comprehension is lost.
Year-End: The student asks relevant questions during reading to clarify main ideas and details, skims to find evidence for predictions and inferences, and applies self-correction strategies with prompting when comprehension breaks down.
Student Statement: I can notice when I’m lost and ask myself a question.
Conditions: Shared class texts with stop-and-check points marked.
Look Fors:
## Attention Strategies
- Asks a question about the main idea at a stop point.
## Knowledge Strategies
- Makes predictions from context and prior knowledge; looks back for evidence when asked.
## Monitoring Strategies
- Notices a breakdown and uses one fix-up strategy when prompted.
Awareness - Student Quote: I asked myself, ‘What’s this paragraph mostly about?’
Evidence Opportunities: Sticky-note questions during reading, reviewed in a conference.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust and use a wide variety of strategies to make meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Attention Strategies: Use relevant questioning during reading to clarify understanding of the main ideas and supporting details.
Knowledge Strategies: Skim texts to locate textual evidence for predictions and inferences.
Monitoring Strategies: Apply self-correction strategies with prompting when comprehension is lost.
Year-End: The student asks relevant questions during reading to clarify main ideas and details, skims to find evidence for predictions and inferences, and applies self-correction strategies with prompting when comprehension breaks down.
Student Statement: I can ask good questions and skim for proof.
Conditions: Longer texts; fewer stop points.
Look Fors:
## Attention Strategies
- Asks questions that separate main ideas from details.
## Knowledge Strategies
- Skims headings, first sentences, and key words to find evidence for a prediction.
## Monitoring Strategies
- Chooses a fix-up strategy when prompted.
Awareness - Student Quote: I skimmed for ‘because’ to find out why she left.
Evidence Opportunities: A skim-and-find task plus a question log.

Skill Descriptor: Adjust and use a wide variety of strategies to make meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Attention Strategies: Use relevant questioning during reading to clarify understanding of the main ideas and supporting details.
Knowledge Strategies: Skim texts to locate textual evidence for predictions and inferences.
Monitoring Strategies: Apply self-correction strategies with prompting when comprehension is lost.
Year-End: The student asks relevant questions during reading to clarify main ideas and details, skims to find evidence for predictions and inferences, and applies self-correction strategies with prompting when comprehension breaks down.
Student Statement: I can use questions and skimming to keep my understanding on track.
Conditions: Varied, more complex texts.
Look Fors:
## Attention Strategies
- Asks relevant questions while reading, mostly without prompting.
## Knowledge Strategies
- Skims efficiently to find evidence for inferences.
## Monitoring Strategies
- Applies self-correction with a light prompt.
Awareness - Student Quote: I wasn’t sure who ‘they’ was, so I skimmed back and found it was the soldiers.
Evidence Opportunities: A think-aloud with a challenging text; the teacher notes questions asked and strategies used.
Left for June: Using questioning, skimming, and self-correction consistently across text types, including unfamiliar ones.

Skill Descriptor: Reflect and respond personally to a variety of texts across genres, interests, and complexities.
Achievement Indicators:
Preferences: Support preferences for and personal reactions to particular texts, authors, illustrators, and genres with details/examples.
Connections: Explain relationships among texts, personal experiences and prior knowledge to draw conclusions or make comparisons supported by relevant details.
Year-End: The student supports preferences and reactions with details and examples, and explains relationships among texts, experiences, and prior knowledge to draw conclusions or make comparisons supported by relevant details.
Student Statement: I can explain why a text worked for me.
Conditions: Self-selected independent reading; reading journal.
Look Fors:
## Preferences
- Explains preferences using features of the text (characters, suspense, style).
## Connections
- Makes personal connections that help them understand a character or event.
Awareness - Student Quote: I like this series because every chapter ends on a cliffhanger.
Evidence Opportunities: A reading journal entry and a book talk with a partner.

Skill Descriptor: Reflect and respond personally to a variety of texts across genres, interests, and complexities.
Achievement Indicators:
Preferences: Support preferences for and personal reactions to particular texts, authors, illustrators, and genres with details/examples.
Connections: Explain relationships among texts, personal experiences and prior knowledge to draw conclusions or make comparisons supported by relevant details.
Year-End: The student supports preferences and reactions with details and examples, and explains relationships among texts, experiences, and prior knowledge to draw conclusions or make comparisons supported by relevant details.
Student Statement: I can back up my reactions with examples.
Conditions: Independent reading plus assigned genres students might not choose.
Look Fors:
## Preferences
- Supports a reaction with specific details or examples from the text.
- Explains a reaction to a less-preferred genre.
## Connections
- Explains how two texts, or a text and an experience, relate to each other.
Awareness - Student Quote: The part where he hides the letter made me angry because he had promised not to lie again.
Evidence Opportunities: Journal prompts: “What part made you react? What does it connect to?”

Skill Descriptor: Reflect and respond personally to a variety of texts across genres, interests, and complexities.
Achievement Indicators:
Preferences: Support preferences for and personal reactions to particular texts, authors, illustrators, and genres with details/examples.
Connections: Explain relationships among texts, personal experiences and prior knowledge to draw conclusions or make comparisons supported by relevant details.
Year-End: The student supports preferences and reactions with details and examples, and explains relationships among texts, experiences, and prior knowledge to draw conclusions or make comparisons supported by relevant details.
Student Statement: I can compare texts and experiences to draw conclusions.
Conditions: A range of genres and complexities read across the year; reading log available.
Look Fors:
## Preferences
- Supports preferences across authors, illustrators, or genres with details and examples.
## Connections
- Explains relationships among texts, experiences, and prior knowledge to draw a conclusion or make a comparison; support is relevant but sometimes thin.
Awareness - Student Quote: Both main characters had to leave home, but only one chose to. That’s why the second book felt more hopeful to me.
Evidence Opportunities: A comparison response or book recommendation drawing on two texts and an experience.
Left for June: Consistently drawing well-supported conclusions and comparisons across genres and complexities, not only favourites.

Skill Descriptor: Independently select, read, and examine critically a range of texts representing all voices.
Achievement Indicators:
Interpretations: Cite evidence to: (1) demonstrate the use of literary elements (plot, setting, characters, conflict, point of view). (2) interpret a text or distinguish between claims supported by facts and claims supported by opinion.
Perspectives: Use a variety of texts with various worldviews to present an alternative perspective on a topic.
Year-End: The student independently selects and critically reads a range of texts representing all voices, cites evidence to show how literary elements work, to interpret a text, and to distinguish fact-supported from opinion-supported claims, and uses texts with various worldviews to present an alternative perspective on a topic.
Student Statement: I can explain a text using its parts and notice whose voice is missing.
Conditions: Choice from a curated, diverse set of texts; small-group discussion.
Look Fors:
## Interpretations
- Explains an interpretation using literary elements, with some evidence.
- Identifies point of view (first person, third person).
- Separates supported from unsupported claims in clear examples.
## Perspectives
- Identifies whose voices are present and whose are missing.
Awareness - Student Quote: It’s all from the coach’s side. We never hear what the new player thought.
Evidence Opportunities: A literature-circle discussion with a perspective role; a fact/opinion sort from an article.

Skill Descriptor: Independently select, read, and examine critically a range of texts representing all voices.
Achievement Indicators:
Interpretations: Cite evidence to: (1) demonstrate the use of literary elements (plot, setting, characters, conflict, point of view). (2) interpret a text or distinguish between claims supported by facts and claims supported by opinion.
Perspectives: Use a variety of texts with various worldviews to present an alternative perspective on a topic.
Year-End: The student independently selects and critically reads a range of texts representing all voices, cites evidence to show how literary elements work, to interpret a text, and to distinguish fact-supported from opinion-supported claims, and uses texts with various worldviews to present an alternative perspective on a topic.
Student Statement: I can cite evidence for how a text works.
Conditions: Longer literary and informational texts; increasing choice in selection.
Look Fors:
## Interpretations
- Cites evidence to show how a literary element, including point of view, shapes the story.
- Distinguishes claims supported by facts from claims supported by opinion, with evidence.
## Perspectives
- Finds a text that offers a different worldview on a topic, with guidance.
Awareness - Description: Explains the effect of point of view.
Awareness - Student Quote: Because it’s told by the sister, we only see what she sees, so we don’t find out about the accident until she does.
Evidence Opportunities: A short written analysis citing two pieces of evidence; a claim-sorting task with an informational text.

Skill Descriptor: Independently select, read, and examine critically a range of texts representing all voices.
Achievement Indicators:
Interpretations: Cite evidence to: (1) demonstrate the use of literary elements (plot, setting, characters, conflict, point of view). (2) interpret a text or distinguish between claims supported by facts and claims supported by opinion.
Perspectives: Use a variety of texts with various worldviews to present an alternative perspective on a topic.
Year-End: The student independently selects and critically reads a range of texts representing all voices, cites evidence to show how literary elements work, to interpret a text, and to distinguish fact-supported from opinion-supported claims, and uses texts with various worldviews to present an alternative perspective on a topic.
Student Statement: I can use different worldviews to present another side.
Conditions: Student-selected texts from a wide, diverse library; mostly independent.
Look Fors:
## Interpretations
- Cites evidence to interpret a text and to judge claims, with occasional prompting for the strongest evidence.
## Perspectives
- Uses two or more texts with different worldviews to present an alternative perspective on a topic.
Awareness - Student Quote: Most articles call it a new park, but the elder’s story shows it was already an important place.
Evidence Opportunities: A short oral or written piece presenting an alternative perspective, drawing on texts with different worldviews.
Left for June: Selecting texts independently across all voices, and citing the strongest evidence without prompting.

Skill Descriptor: Analyze the characteristics, language, form, features, and genre of a range of texts.
Achievement Indicators:
Text Features (Literary Knowledge): Identify the characteristics of different genres, both literary and informational, including the characteristics that signal a text may be AI-generated.
Text Impact (Author’s Craft): Compare the methods used by different writers on similar topics.
Year-End: The student identifies the characteristics of literary and informational genres, including those that signal a text may be AI-generated, and compares the methods different writers use on similar topics.
Student Statement: I can identify a genre by its features.
Conditions: Clear examples of familiar genres; anchor charts.
Look Fors:
## Text Features
- Identifies common text structures and the features of familiar literary and informational genres.
- Recognizes obvious signs that a text may be AI-generated, using a checklist.
## Text Impact
- Identifies a writer’s choice and the purpose it serves.
Awareness - Student Quote: It’s a news article because it answers who, what, where, and when at the start.
Evidence Opportunities: A genre sort with short texts, including one AI-generated example.

Text Impact (Author’s Craft): Compare the methods used by different writers on similar topics.
Year-End: The student identifies the characteristics of literary and informational genres, including those that signal a text may be AI-generated, and compares the methods different writers use on similar topics.
Student Statement: I can compare how two writers handle the same topic.
Conditions: Paired texts on similar topics in different genres.
Look Fors:
## Text Features
- Identifies characteristics of a wider range of genres (opinion piece, memoir, report, poem).
- Explains one or two signals that a text may be AI-generated.
## Text Impact
- Compares one method two writers use (opening, word choice, evidence, structure).
Awareness - Student Quote: The poem uses one image to make you feel it; the article uses numbers to make you believe it.
Evidence Opportunities: A paired-text comparison chart of the writers’ methods.

Look Fors:

Skill Descriptor: Develop strategies to enhance clarity in written works.
Achievement Indicators:
Identity: Identify strengths as a writer and independently set goals for improvement.
Intention: Demonstrate initiative by enhancing ideas through experiments with genre, form, and style.
Development: Experiment with a variety of writing and design processes to plan, develop, and create texts, and identify where AI tools may help or hinder.
Response: Use mentor texts, exemplars, and feedback to reflect on and apply self-assessment skills.
Year-End: The student names strengths and independently sets goals, experiments with genre, form, and style to enhance ideas, tries a variety of processes to plan, develop, and create texts while judging where AI tools help or hinder, and uses mentor texts, exemplars, and feedback to self-assess.
Student Statement: I can name my strengths and set a goal with my teacher.
Conditions: Writing workshop routines; regular conferences; process tools available.
Look Fors:
## Identity
- Names specific strengths with an example; sets a goal with the teacher.
## Intention
- Brings ideas from their own experience into writing.
## Development
- Plans, drafts, and revises with guidance.
- Shares an opinion on whether an AI tool would help with a task.
## Response
- Identifies craft moves in mentor texts and their own writing during conferences.
Awareness - Description: Names a strength and a goal.
Awareness - Student Quote: I’m good at dialogue, but my middles drag. I want to cut what doesn’t matter.
Evidence Opportunities: A writer’s profile with strengths and a first goal, plus a conference record.

Skill Descriptor: Create a variety of texts with purpose and understand the influence of the writer/creator.
Achievement Indicators:
Topic/Idea: Define a clear topic or idea that stays focused throughout.
Development: Develop a topic/idea by incorporating relevant details and evidence, being transparent about where the evidence came from.
Reasoning: Use information to help the reader understand the writer’s reasoning.
Year-End: The student creates a variety of texts with a clear, focused topic or idea, develops it with relevant details and evidence while being transparent about sources, uses information to help the reader follow the reasoning, and understands how a writer’s choices influence the reader.
Student Statement: I can write with a clear idea and support it.
Conditions: Familiar forms; multi-paragraph pieces.
Look Fors:
## Topic/Idea
- Defines a clear idea; may drift in longer pieces.
## Development
- Uses relevant details and examples.
- Notes where information came from when asked.
## Reasoning
- Presents straightforward reasoning in familiar forms.
Awareness - Description: Explains one choice and its effect.
Awareness - Student Quote: I started with a question so the reader would want to know the answer.
Evidence Opportunities: A short piece in a familiar form with a writer’s note on one choice.

Conditions: A variety of forms; students choose some purposes.
Look Fors:
## Topic/Idea
- Maintains a clear focus in most pieces.
## Development
- Develops ideas with relevant details and evidence, transparent about sources; may rely on one source.

- Uses information to lead the reader through the reasoning; links are sometimes left for the reader to make.
Awareness - Description: Explains the influence of a choice.
Awareness - Student Quote: I put the strongest fact last so it would stick with the reader.
Evidence Opportunities: A piece in a student-chosen form for a given purpose, with an author’s note on how they guided the reader.
Left for June: Sustained focus and transparent, well-linked reasoning across a variety of forms.

Skill Descriptor: Select an appropriate form that reflects audience, purpose, and topic.
Achievement Indicators:
Structure: Maintain organizational structure throughout
Sequence: Arrange evidence with a logical sequence through mostly controlled pacing.
Transition: Use transition words and phrases to show connections.
Leads/Conclusions: Address the purpose with an adequate lead and conclusion.
Year-End: The student selects a form that suits the audience, purpose, and topic, maintains its structure throughout, sequences evidence logically with mostly controlled pacing, uses transitions to show connections, and writes leads and conclusions that address the purpose.
Student Statement: I can organize my writing in a form that fits.
Conditions: Familiar forms; organizers available.
Look Fors:
## Structure
- Chooses a basic structure that fits the purpose; may lose it partway through.
## Sequence
- Orders ideas in a helpful way.
## Transition
- Uses predictable transitions (first, next, in conclusion).
## Leads/ Conclusions
- Includes a lead and conclusion, usually formulaic.
Awareness - Student Quote: I used steps because I’m teaching how to do it.
Evidence Opportunities: A short piece checked against a structure checklist.

Skill Descriptor: Select an appropriate form that reflects audience, purpose, and topic.

Student Statement: I can keep my structure and connect my ideas.
Conditions: Longer pieces in two or three forms; mentor texts for leads and transitions.
Look Fors:
## Structure
- Maintains the structure through most of a piece.
## Sequence
- Arranges evidence in a logical order; pacing is uneven (rushed or dragging in places).
## Transition

Evidence Opportunities: A revision of leads and transitions in a draft, with the original and revised versions side by side.

Skill Descriptor: Select an appropriate form that reflects audience, purpose, and topic.

Student Statement: I can choose a form and carry it through.
Conditions: Student-chosen forms for a given audience and purpose.
Look Fors:
## Structure
- Maintains organizational structure throughout most pieces.
## Sequence
- Sequences evidence logically with mostly controlled pacing.
## Transition
- Uses transitions to show connections between ideas and paragraphs.
## Leads/ Conclusions
- Writes an adequate lead and conclusion that address the purpose, in planned pieces.
Awareness - Student Quote: I sped through the boring part so I could slow down at the rescue.
Evidence Opportunities: A piece in a student-chosen form with a planning sheet showing structure and sequence.
Left for June: Maintaining structure and pacing in on-demand writing and less familiar forms.

Skill Descriptor: Include interesting and/or domain-specific words and phrases to convey and enhance meaning.
Achievement Indicators:
Specific & Accurate Words: Give deliberate attention to choices with evidence of stretch to unique choices.
Striking Words & Phrases: Use common figurative language and imagery (simile, metaphor, personification, dialogue).
Deepening Meaning: Convey a meaning that is easy to understand.
Year-End: The student makes deliberate word choices with some stretch toward unique ones, uses common figurative language and imagery, and conveys a meaning that is easy to understand.
Student Statement: I can choose words on purpose.
Conditions: Familiar topics; word banks and mentor sentences available.
Look Fors:
## Specific & Accurate Words
- Chooses specific words over general ones during revision.
## Striking Words & Phrases
- Uses sensory details to create imagery.
## Deepening Meaning
- Chooses words suited to the audience and text type.
Awareness - Student Quote: I changed ‘walked’ to ‘trudged’ because she was tired.
Evidence Opportunities: A short descriptive paragraph; students highlight three words chosen on purpose.

Skill Descriptor: Include interesting and/or domain-specific words and phrases to convey and enhance meaning.

Student Statement: I can stretch my word choices and use figurative language.

Look Fors:
## Specific & Accurate Words
- Tries less common or domain-specific words, sometimes misusing one.
## Striking Words & Phrases
- Uses simile, metaphor, personification, or dialogue to show something.
## Deepening Meaning
- Meaning stays clear in most places.
Awareness - Student Quote: I said the hallway swallowed him to show how small he felt.
Evidence Opportunities: A revision task: replace five general words and add one figurative phrase, then note the effect.

Awareness - Student Quote: I took out the second metaphor because it made the ending confusing.
Evidence Opportunities: Two short pieces on one topic for different audiences, with a note on word choices.
Left for June: Consistent deliberate choices across forms, and stretch choices that always keep the meaning clear.

Skill Descriptor: Provide evidence of author’s style, personality, and experience.
Achievement Indicators:
Audience Engagement: Address the audience and topic/idea/ purpose in a sincere way.
Tone: Experiment with creating a tone that supports and clarifies.
Commitment: Commit to the topic convincingly due to the care shown in crafting the piece.
Style: Use the appropriate point of view, differentiating between formal and informal writing.
Year-End: The student addresses the audience and purpose sincerely, experiments with tone that supports and clarifies, commits to the topic convincingly through care in crafting, and uses an appropriate point of view, differentiating formal from informal writing.
Student Statement: I can write in a way that sounds like me.
Conditions: Personal and assigned topics; mentor texts with strong voice.
Look Fors:
## Audience Engagement
- Connects the reader to the topic, especially at the start.
## Tone
- Uses a tone that fits the audience and purpose in planned pieces.
## Commitment
- Shows commitment to the topic, with some vague generalities.
## Style
- Experiments with point of view.
Awareness - Student Quote: You can tell it’s me because I made the kind of joke I’d make.
Evidence Opportunities: A personal piece; a partner finishes the sentence “I can tell you care about this because...”

Skill Descriptor: Provide evidence of author’s style, personality, and experience.

- Uses specific details and examples that show care for the topic.

- Tells formal from informal writing and adjusts point of view and register.

- Addresses the audience and purpose sincerely in most pieces.
## Tone

- Commits to the topic convincingly through careful crafting, with occasional generalities.

Evidence Opportunities: A piece for a real audience with an author’s note: reader, tone, and point of view.

Skill Descriptor: Include well-crafted sentences to support meaning and readability.

Variety: Use a variety of sentence lengths and beginnings to create clarity.
Rhythm: Create a rhythm that is easy to read aloud.
Year-End: The student writes simple, compound, and complex sentences that bring clarity, varies sentence lengths and beginnings for clarity, and creates a rhythm that is easy to read aloud.

Look Fors:
## Crafted Structure
- Writes correct simple and compound sentences; complex sentences are attempted, sometimes with errors.
## Variety
- Uses a routine variety of lengths and beginnings.
## Rhythm
- Reads smoothly after revision; mechanical in places.
Awareness - Description: Hears a problem when reading aloud.
Awareness - Student Quote: Every sentence starts with ‘Then,’ so it sounds like a list.
Evidence Opportunities: A writing sample analyzed for sentence types and first words, then read aloud to a partner.

Skill Descriptor: Demonstrate correct spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and grammar usage.
Achievement Indicators:
Spelling: Use spelling/phonetic rules to attempt difficult words.
Punctuation: Use common internal punctuation correctly (semi-colon, colon).
Grammar: Use common grammar structures and capitalization (verb tense consistency, dialogue).
References: Underline and/or italicize the names of books, articles, and websites.

Student Statement: I can edit for the basics.
Conditions: Editing checklist; mini-lessons begin on semicolons and colons.
Look Fors:
## Spelling
- Spells common words correctly; attempts difficult words phonetically.
## Punctuation
- Uses commas, quotation marks, and apostrophes mostly correctly; semicolons and colons are new.
## Grammar
- Uses basic agreement and capitalization; verb tense sometimes shifts.
## References
- Names a book, article, or website when used, without special formatting.
Awareness - Student Quote: I’m checking that I didn’t switch from past to present.
Evidence Opportunities: A November on-demand sample analyzed for conventions; one editing goal set.

Skill Descriptor: Use language of harmony and respect, self-monitoring and adjusting as appropriate.

Skill Descriptor: Seek and respond to questions to clarify or explain ideas, concepts, problems, and solutions.

Skill Descriptor: Give and respond to a variety of directions and instructions.

- Follows multi-step instructions that require decisions.

Skill Descriptor: Give and respond to a variety of directions and instructions.

Skill Descriptor: Construct meaning from a variety of text considering the source, intended audience, and purpose.

Literal Understanding: Use knowledge of common figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, idiom, imagery) to contribute to understanding a text.
Inferential Understanding: Identify the overarching idea and supporting details of a text, providing textual evidence to support their inference.
Text Intention: Explain how genre and text structures support the writer’s purpose.

Look Fors:

- Compares the stated purposes of two writers on the same topic.

Evidence Opportunities: A main-idea organizer with quoted evidence.

Monitoring Strategies: Apply self-correction strategies efficiently and independently.

Look Fors:
## Attention Strategies
- Summarizes key information at the end of a section, with an organizer.
## Knowledge Strategies

Skill Descriptor: Independently select, read, and examine critically construct meaning from a range of texts representing all voices.
Achievement Indicators:
Interpretations: Reflect on the choices of: (1) literary elements (plot, setting, characters, conflict, point of view) to contribute to the meaning of a text. (2) reasons to support a claim and identify irrelevant information, recognizing that AI-generated texts may introduce plausible-sounding but unsupported claims that require the same scrutiny as any other source.
Perspectives: Detect prejudice, stereotyping, and bias, and how language is used to manipulate, persuade, or control, recognizing that these patterns can appear in AI-generated content, which may reflect biases embedded in training data without any clear author.
Year-End: The student independently selects and critically reads texts representing all voices, reflects on how literary elements contribute to meaning, evaluates reasons for a claim and identifies irrelevant information (scrutinizing AI-generated claims like any source), and detects prejudice, stereotyping, bias, and manipulative language, including in AI-generated content.
Student Statement: I can cite evidence and present another perspective.
Conditions: Curated, diverse texts; literature circles.
Look Fors:
## Interpretations
- Cites evidence to show how literary elements work.
- Distinguishes claims supported by facts from those supported by opinion.
## Perspectives
- Uses texts with different worldviews to present another perspective.
- Recognizes obvious stereotypes.
Awareness - Student Quote: The only farmer in the book is shown as not smart. That’s a stereotype.
Evidence Opportunities: A literature-circle discussion and a fact/opinion claim sort.

Skill Descriptor: Critically analyze the characteristics, language, form, features, and genre of a range of texts.

Look Fors:
## Text Features
- Identifies characteristics of literary and informational genres, including signs a text may be AI-generated.
## Text Impact
- Compares methods writers use on similar topics.
Awareness - Student Quote: Memoirs use ‘I’ and real memories, so you trust them differently.
Evidence Opportunities: A genre feature sort and paired-text comparison.

Year-End: The student sets stylistic goals drawn from a variety of genres and forms, works on their craft by bringing in their identity and learning, breaks tasks into manageable parts (with or without a traditional process), decides when AI tools can enhance a part, and uses mentor texts, exemplars, and feedback at every stage.

Conditions: Writing workshop; conferences; mentor texts.
Look Fors:
## Identity
- Names strengths and sets improvement goals independently.
## Intention
